title: Rejoining UNIDO: Reform, Value and Climate Finance
label: 15 September 2026 · UNIDO evidence
summary: The committee questioned Matt Toombs and Paul Durrant from the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero about why the UK should rejoin UNIDO after leaving in 2012. The witnesses argued that UNIDO has genuinely reformed and that the UK's relationship with it has deepened through programmes on green industrialisation. They faced tough questions about the value for money, access to climate finance for the poorest, and how to prevent backsliding, and confirmed a UK review of the decision would take place in 2029.

speakers.label: Matt Toombs
speakers.name: Matt Toombs
speakers.role: Director for International Net Zero - Climate Finance and Strategy, Department for Energy Security and Net Zero

speakers.label: Paul Durrant
speakers.name: Paul Durrant
speakers.role: Head of the International Green Industrialisation, Technology Innovation & Electrification (IGNITE) team, Department for Energy Security and Net Zero

chapters.title: The case for rejoining
chapters.takeaway: The government believes the context and the UK's relationship with UNIDO have changed enough to justify rejoining.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thanks for coming. The obvious question is: why rejoin UNIDO at all? We seem to have a good relationship without being a member, and it works well as a delivery agent. And what genuine reforms justify reversing the decision to leave 15 years ago?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: The context now is very different from 2012. Our relationship with UNIDO has also changed a lot, especially over the last five years of programme engagement. Clean, green industrial development is critical for developing countries, and the UK can benefit from being part of that growth. Back in 2012 we had no programmes with UNIDO and a thin relationship. Since then we've worked closely with them through COP26, on green public procurement with India, on the Accelerate-to-Demonstrate programme worth about £125 million, and on industrial decarbonisation with Brazil. So the value of rejoining is much greater now.

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: On reforms: UNIDO is smaller and more efficient than it was at the time of the 2011 multilateral aid review. It's more transparent and open, with an independent evaluation unit and regular publications on programme effectiveness. There's much more disclosure than before. Those are some of the reasons we think it's worth moving.

chapters.title: What about other countries?
chapters.takeaway: Other countries that left may also return, but the UK is not alone in staying engaged.

turns.speaker: Baroness Anelay of St Johns
turns.text: You've said the context has changed. What about other countries that left? Have you talked to them about returning? If they're not considering it, why not, given the benefits you describe?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: We're in conversation with like-minded countries about their relationship with UNIDO. I can't speak for them, but a number of industrialised countries remain members—Japan, Italy, Germany, and the EU all have strong relationships. We wouldn't be an exception. And we're not starting from scratch; we've been building this relationship for at least five years.

turns.speaker: Baroness Anelay of St Johns
turns.text: Some countries still think it's not worth joining and being part of governance, even if they contribute. Without naming them, do you think others that left might rejoin?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: Yes, I do. Next week at the UN General Assembly and Climate Week NYC there will be discussions on green industrialisation. It's a priority for the Turkish COP31 presidency and the Ethiopian COP32 presidency. We've built confidence through programmes, and we'd expect other countries to take a similar route.

chapters.title: Climate finance and the poorest
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses argue UNIDO membership can help scale up climate finance, but admit access remains difficult.

turns.speaker: Lord Boateng
turns.text: Japan, Italy and Germany have always been strong on industrial policy and their economies thrived. But we've spent billions on aid with insufficient impact for the poorest. Now our development budget is cut, and we're being asked to pay a UNIDO subscription. How will membership help people facing climate and water crises? Less than 3% of global climate finance goes to water and sanitation, and only 0.3% to water, waste and hygiene. Girls miss school because they lack decent toilets. How will UNIDO membership improve things for the most marginalised?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: I agree it's crucial that our international climate finance supports those who need it most. Our climate finance is smaller now, so we've had to prioritise. The government published an updated ICF strategy this year, showing we need money to go further and mobilise larger amounts.

turns.speaker: Lord Boateng
turns.text: That's all very well, but how does UNIDO membership help people on the ground who can't access green climate finance?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: Being a member helps us get scale—transforming outcomes rather than just small projects. For example, with Brazil, about £15 million of UK investment alongside their industrial development led to them accessing £250 million of wider international finance, expected to raise around £2 billion in private finance. That changes livelihoods and creates jobs.

turns.speaker: Baroness Verma
turns.text: Is it time to revisit how climate finance is accessed? People on the ground say it's complicated, slow, and full of hurdles, so those who need it most don't get it. And is ODA fit for purpose this century?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: Access to finance is a real challenge. The UK has worked with the Green Climate Fund and others to speed up and improve access. It's a priority across our climate finance work. It's a wider ODA challenge, not specific to UNIDO. With smaller ODA budgets, we need to use money where it can have scale and mobilise wider finance.

turns.speaker: Baroness Verma
turns.text: Are you restricted in how you spend ODA with private companies? To get private investment, ODA needs to be easier for businesses to navigate, otherwise you won't get scale-up.

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: We absolutely agree that connecting private finance and the private sector with publicly financed activities is critical. We have many examples with UNIDO involving UK businesses—like the green tea facility in Kenya or green steel in South Africa. The private sector has to be fully part of the solution.

chapters.title: Engagement with other countries
chapters.takeaway: The UK discusses industrial development with Australia and New Zealand, but won't comment on their UNIDO plans.

turns.speaker: Baroness Lawlor
turns.text: You mentioned Japan, but what about the US, Australia and New Zealand? Have you engaged with them? Are they likely to rejoin?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: I don't want to speak for individual countries. The US position on climate change is well known.

turns.speaker: Lord Boateng
turns.text: The US doesn't believe in it. What's the position of USAID and the FCDO, which used to work closely together?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: We work with the US where we can, but clearly on development and ODA, the US has withdrawn from agencies and reduced funding.

turns.speaker: Baroness Lawlor
turns.text: What about Australia and New Zealand?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: We work closely with both. Australia has the COP presidency with Turkey this year and will oversee industrial development discussions. We talk to them as partners.

turns.speaker: Baroness Lawlor
turns.text: Do you know if Australia is going back?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: I wouldn't want to comment on their specific relationship with UNIDO.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: It might be interesting to see if any statements have been made about that.

chapters.title: Preventing backsliding and reviewing membership
chapters.takeaway: The UK will review the benefits of rejoining in 2029, but it's a UK review, not a UNIDO one.

turns.speaker: Lord Hannay of Chiswick
turns.text: I was British ambassador to the UN in the 1990s. We're told UNIDO is reforming well. If we rejoin, how do we ensure it doesn't slip backwards? The FAO had a high reputation after the war but by the 1990s was a rest home for politicians and wasted money. Also, UN organisations turf fight. How do we stop UNIDO doing that? And have we set up a review after a fixed term, say five years, to check it's still improving? Will you come back to this committee?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: We wouldn't assume things won't slip backwards. Being a member gives us greater engagement and oversight, and stronger levers to act if things go wrong. That's part of the case for rejoining.

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: On turf fighting, the UN80 context is important—many agencies are undergoing challenging reforms and will become more streamlined. Being part of UNIDO lets us ensure it's run effectively.

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: On review: we plan to review whether we're achieving the benefits of rejoining in 2029. That relates to our funding agreement with UNIDO. In 2029 we'll look at whether we've met the tests we're setting now.

turns.speaker: Lord Hannay of Chiswick
turns.text: That will depend on whether we sustain membership or decide to withdraw again.

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: Our intention is to make rejoining a positive move and sustain the relationship. But it's right to review whether we're achieving the benefits in three years.

turns.speaker: Lord Hannay of Chiswick
turns.text: If Parliament is involved in reviewing, would that help your hand in UNIDO governance?

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We'd be keen to participate, but can you commit to that today? Is the review point set in the agreement?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: The review point is for the UK to decide, not part of a formal agreement with UNIDO.

turns.speaker: Lord Hannay of Chiswick
turns.text: That's what I meant: a UK review of the UK's decision to rejoin, not a UNIDO review that ends with hundreds of pages and little action.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We'll end the public session here as we're tight for time.
